talks.title: 12. EDR Evasion and OODA Loops by Jackson T.
talks.teaser: Uses the OODA decision loop to explain how operators and EDR sensors make choices, and where evasion fits in each step.
talks.summary:
The talk applies John Boyd's observe, orient, decide, act cycle, originally developed from fighter pilot analysis, to red team operations. The speaker describes how operators gather information from the target and from outside sources, how tools automate parts of that gathering, and how candidate attack paths are weighed against constraints set by an engagement's tradecraft policy. Matthew Monty's principles, including knowledge, innovation, awareness, precaution, operational security and program security, serve as a way to frame those constraints.

A worked internal penetration test scenario shows the loop in practice. Service account credentials and an active jump box session offer two routes to a crown jewel server. Because the EDR is good at flagging suspicious command lines but little else, the operator avoids API-based LSASS dumping and instead uses Task Manager over RDP. The speaker then turns the same model on the EDR sensor. It observes through kernel callbacks, user-mode hooks and ETW, builds a situation model, matches events against behavioral signatures or ML models, decides based on its configuration, and acts through separate components. Case studies include attack surface reduction rules for Windows Defender recovered from resource files, and a published file classification model probed for biases that let padded malicious binaries evade it.

The closing recommendations cover identifying the telemetry sources of products you face, learning how telemetry moves between sensor components, studying on-sensor signatures and design limits, and building an offline telemetry back end in a lab. Quantifying tradecraft policy can help operators tighten the gap between what they observe and what they choose.

talks.title: 10. How to make intelligence, hunting, and response BFFs by Kamil Bojarski
talks.teaser: Explains how to write intelligence requirements that align threat intel with incident response and SOC detection teams.
talks.summary:
The talk tackles the gap between threat intelligence teams and the security operations, incident response and hunting teams they support. Kamil Bojarski argues that intelligence work often drifts into polished reports that front-line staff have no easy way to use, which turns the team into overhead. He cites a 2021 cyber threat intelligence survey in which roughly 30 to 40 percent of respondents had documented intelligence requirements, and says intelligence staff contribute too little to writing them.

He proposes judging each intelligence product by three questions: who receives it and how closely their teams sit to intelligence in the organization, how the output is consumed technically (manual parsing versus automated feeds of indicators), and whether it fits daily work at all. Feedback loops should run both ways between intelligence, monitoring, incident response and hunting. For SOC analysts, indicators should arrive in a format their tools ingest, and when manual entry is unavoidable, only the critical ones should be pushed. For responders, reports should describe activity in artifacts they already examine, such as process trees and memory forensics output. For hunters, behaviour should be expressed as command-line patterns in the logs they actually collect.

The bottom line is that intelligence value comes from fitting into other teams' workflows, not only from technical accuracy or timeliness. Requirements tailored to each team also show whether a gap justifies building in-house intelligence or can be covered by consuming vendor reporting.

talks.title: 08. What the F#*%? by Chris Truncer and Joe Leon
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for 08. What the F#*%? by Chris Truncer and Joe Leon.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Chris Truncer and Joe Leon from Forty North Security present their exploration of F# as an offensive security tool, motivated by a December 2020 penetration test where traditional app whitelisting bypasses failed. Facing strong defensive controls (ATP, Bit9 app whitelisting), they discovered F# as a viable alternative to C# for establishing C2 communications and executing post-exploitation code, particularly by leveraging the Microsoft-signed FSI (F# Scripting Console).

## Key Topics

**F# Language Fundamentals**: F# is a functional-oriented, strongly-typed language designed for effective function writing. It automatically infers data types (similar to Python) and allows mixing .NET code. The speakers note that while F# syntax is considered difficult to learn and not intuitive for C#/PowerShell developers, it can be effectively weaponized for offensive purposes.

**FSI (F# Scripting Console) as a Bypass**: The F# scripting console, a Microsoft-signed binary, bypassed Bit9 app whitelisting where traditional methods (MSBuild, gadgets-to-JSScript, WimMc, Ghost loader) failed. They identified four required DLL dependencies (fsharp.compiler.interactive.settings, fsharp.compiler.private, fsharpcore, microsoft.build.utilities.core) and successfully executed shellcode injection templates, establishing C2 after four hours of testing.

**Execute Assembly with F#**: Extending the execute assembly concept (unmanaged code loading managed code via CLR), the speakers explored loading F# assemblies in-memory. They encountered invoke-3 errors and fsharpcore.dll dependency issues, testing four solutions: standalone assemblies (too large at 1.5+ MB), dropping DLLs to disk, global assembly cache installation (requires admin), and dynamic dependency resolution.

## Technical Details

**AppDomain.AssemblyResolve Solution**: The breakthrough came through Jean Maes' research on AppDomain.AssemblyResolve—a callback function that fires when the CLR cannot locate an assembly. The speakers embedded fsharpcore.dll bytes directly in code and modified the open-source "hosting CLR" C++ project to dynamically resolve dependencies without disk drops or elevated privileges. This approach completely eliminated dependency resolution errors and enabled true in-memory F# execution.

**Compilation Methods**: FSI.exe location varies by installation path (Program Files/x86/Visual Studio/.../F#/ or .NET SDK 5.0.103 folder). The --standalone flag theoretically embeds dependencies but generates 1.5+ MB binaries and doesn't actually create standalone executables as documented; it produces a loader executable plus separate DLL. This remains a noted limitation.

**Shellcode Injection Templates**: Released templates include basic shellcode injection (Vincent Yiu's original 2018 template), remote process injection via CreateRemoteThread, and QueueUserAPC variants. PInvoke (Platform Invoke) enables Win32 API calls; F# byte array syntax differs significantly from C# (0xhex format with "uy" suffix), but functionality remains compatible.

**Defensive Detection**: Matt Graber and Red Canary identified that AMSI can catch embedded F# applications, .NET ETW captures fsharpcore loading, and focus should be on behavioral indicators of .NET execution rather than language specifics. AMSI and ETW bypass techniques (referenced via mdsec blogs and tools like amzeefail.com) remain applicable to F# code.

## Takeaways

F# presents a viable, relatively underfocused offensive alternative to C# due to limited prior adoption in adversary tooling. The AppDomain.AssemblyResolve approach elegantly solves dependency issues, enabling in-memory execution via execute assembly techniques in frameworks like Cobalt Strike. The speakers released a GitHub repository ("What the F") containing modified hosting CLR code, shellcode templates, and execution guides. Future priorities include Beacon Object File (BOF) implementation for seamless Cobalt Strike integration, syscall integration to bypass API hooking, and porting existing C# tools to F#. Defenders should instrument .NET execution telemetry (AMSI/ETW) to detect behavioral indicators rather than language-specific artifacts.

talks.title: 07. Windows 10 TCP/IP RCE - from the patch to the screen of death by Adam 'pi3' Zabrocki
talks.teaser: Shows how a pre-authentication IPv6 Router Advertisement flaw in Windows 10 was turned into a remote crash exploit.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at CVE-2020-16898, a Windows 10 TCP/IP flaw in IPv6 Router Advertisement handling that was patched on 13 October 2020. The speaker explains why it stood out: the packet is parsed before any firewall rule can apply, no authentication is needed, and the code runs in the kernel. Vendors had called exploitation trivial, yet little public exploit code existed in the days after the patch.

Instead of diffing the patch, which bundled dozens of other fixes, the speaker worked from a published detection signature that flagged a bad length value in the RDNSS option. Testing with crafted packets in a debugger showed that the source address had to be link-local, and that an even length value made the parser read the last address bytes as a next header. Hidden headers could then be smuggled inside the option, and reaching the route information path required adjusting size checks. A contiguous-buffer shortcut in the kernel API blocked the overflow until the packets were fragmented, after which the stack was smashed and the machine crashed.

The takeaway is that a pre-authentication parser bug in a mature network stack can still be reachable, and that detection logic can point researchers to the code worth reversing. The speaker published a detailed write-up and the exploit script alongside the talk.

talks.title: 06. Adversary emulation is a fraud by David Hunt
talks.teaser: Argues that vendor-driven complexity distracts security teams from basics like asset inventory, logging and patching.
talks.summary:
The talk, given by David Hunt, argues that security teams are overwhelmed by competing terminology, certifications, open-source tools and frameworks, and that much of this clutter is driven by how vendors sell products to executives who then push them down to practitioners. Using a fictional office scenario, he walks through a red and blue exercise and shows how such exercises often become competitions that fail to answer whether the organization is actually safer afterward.

On adversary emulation specifically, he explains that a small team can only approximate an attacker's tactics using public intelligence and limited time and budget, while nation-state groups have far greater resources. He warns that marketing may promise more than an emulation exercise can deliver. He separates vulnerability, threat and risk, then lays out a basic hygiene sequence: inventory of assets and how they connect, centralized logging, scheduled patching that also covers non-Windows systems, prioritized vulnerability scanning, and practical security education. From his incident response work, he recalls that the network architecture diagrams organizations drew after an attack were usually wrong.

He closes by urging practitioners to ask basic questions about devices, log retention, patch rollout and risk categorization, and to simplify processes rather than chase buzzwords. The takeaway is to focus on foundational security work and treat added complexity as a cost that has to be justified.

talks.title: 05. O Event, Where Art Thou? by Grzegorz Tworek
talks.teaser: Walks through how Windows event logging works internally and how its logs can be blinded, altered, or silently corrupted.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through the Windows event logging infrastructure, including the event categories, per-log access control, and the move from the older EVT format to EVTX in Vista. It notes that the legacy RPC path still coexists with the newer ETW-based one. Reading logs through bookmarks is shown to be costly under heavy event volume, so bulk reads with local parsing or subscriptions are suggested instead.

The demonstrations centre on tampering. A documented event-writing function, wrapped in PowerShell, let a regular user write entries, and disassembly showed it sending an ETW message. Stopping the ETW session behind the System log, using the trace log utility, stopped later events from appearing. The Security log's session is flagged as non-stoppable, so the API returns access denied, and the operating system checks its startup name against a hard-coded value. A registry value that the Windows installer creates, if present at boot, makes auditing record nothing, leaving a gap in history.

Editing an evtx file by hand breaks the CRC32 checksums on its chunks, and Windows silently discards invalid chunks on opening, so most entries vanish without any warning. The takeaways are to manage log sizes, forward events off the host, treat logs from already compromised machines with suspicion, and preserve evidence with parsers that keep the original bytes.

talks.title: 01. Between the Chair and Keyboard - keynote by J Wolfgang Goerlich
talks.teaser: A usability framework aligns user journeys and attacker paths so secure choices feel natural instead of punitive.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with the familiar idea that failures sit “between the chair and keyboard,” then ties that to breach data where most incidents involve people. Drawing on design thinking—notably the argument that “human error” often reflects bad design—the speaker argues security teams blame users instead of studying how paths, steps, and choices shape behavior.

The core model examines workforce journeys (length, familiarity, friction, cognitive load) alongside adversary paths. Examples span everyday email login, MFA inconsistency, phishing reporting, DLP rollout blowback, IAM onboarding bypass metrics, and misuse of customer signup features. Nudges, sludge, smart defaults, and controls invisible to users are contrasted with measures that slow people down; Verizon charting on attacker step counts illustrates raising adversary friction while simplifying legitimate work.

For practitioners, the talk proposes mapping processes with journey or behavior maps, measuring workarounds as design feedback, and troubleshooting failures through ignorance, irrationality, incentives, and investment gaps. Security advocates paired with business champions should close that loop. Phishing simulations that exploit fear or bonuses are questioned; passwordless, push MFA, inbox controls, and device identity are favored where they ease users while confounding criminals. The close compares decades of ergonomic fixes for monitors and keyboards with still blaming people for security mistakes, urging a human-centric reset across usability and defensibility.

talks.title: Introduction to Industrial Control Systems: Build, Break, Secure by Arnaud SOULLIÉ
talks.teaser: Explains industrial control systems, their main components and common weaknesses, and previews a hands-on training course.
talks.summary:
This introduction to industrial control systems starts with where they are used, from power plants and water treatment to pools and building air conditioning. It then breaks down the main parts: sensors that convert physical measurements into electrical signals, actuators that act on the physical world, programmable logic controllers that run the automation logic, and SCADA supervision that centralises remote control. The corporate network is almost always linked to the control network, so that boundary matters.

The middle of the session covers the security picture. The speaker argues that ICS should be judged by its own traits, such as very long equipment lifespans and a strong change-management culture, rather than measured against corporate IT. Recurring weaknesses from assessments include unclear ownership, poor network segmentation, unauthenticated legacy protocols, risky third-party access, difficult patching and weak security monitoring. Two incidents are reviewed: a ransomware attack on a corporate network that forced a fuel pipeline to halt operations, and a small water treatment plant where a weak remote-access password let an intruder change a treatment setting until an operator reset it.

The closing section previews a multi-part hands-on training built around build, break and secure. Students work with virtual machines, a simulated distillation process driven by a PLC simulator and a SCADA application, and a capture-the-flag exercise against a remote home lab with a model train and robotic arms. The aim is to understand how a system works before attacking or defending it.

talks.title: Operational Threat Intelligence by Joe Slowik
talks.teaser: Argues that threat intelligence should support frontline defenders, and previews an operations-focused training course.
talks.summary:
This session previews a three-day operational threat intelligence training. Joe Slowik begins by separating intelligence from popular myths about secrecy, then defines it as methodical collection, analysis and dissemination that helps decision makers. Cyber threat intelligence is presented as a narrower subset focused on adversaries that could harm an organization, serving both strategic leaders and operational staff such as SOC analysts and incident responders.

Slowik argues that much CTI output fails defenders. He points to heavy emphasis on attribution, overly technical reverse engineering write-ups, and bulk indicator lists with short shelf lives. His alternative starts with understanding an organization's value centers and security needs, then studying adversary missions and behaviors, and turning those findings into detection strategies and rules. He notes that the course assumes only free tools and public data, and that paid third-party feeds are worth it mainly for visibility beyond one's own network.

The training covers source assessment for third-party reporting, indicator enrichment and pivoting to understand behavior, and communicating results to responders and IT staff. During questions he addressed red team scoping, making the case to management, and suitability for newcomers from either security or intelligence backgrounds. The takeaway for practitioners is to measure intelligence by the defensive outcomes it improves.

talks.title: 2. Piotr Białczak - Hunting malware using its fingerprints
talks.teaser: Shows how network traffic fingerprints can help hunters find malware families when IP and domain blocklists fail.
talks.summary:
Blocklists of IP addresses and domains lose value fast, since malware rotates infrastructure through techniques like DGA and fast flux, and they fail against unknown threats. The talk proposes fingerprinting network traffic instead, using protocol fields that change rarely and are hard to alter. It separates tools that name a family directly from generic feature extractors, and focuses on the latter and on the trade-off between uniqueness and generalization.

A live demo loaded public packet captures into Kibana with Suricata alerts, then pulled a TLS client fingerprint tied to a command-and-control server. That fingerprint appeared in 51 messages, and exported fingerprints were checked against a public blocklist of such fingerprints. A second demo ran an HTTP fingerprinting tool on requests from one malware family, where each request type produced its own fingerprint. Comparing fingerprint sets from a known capture with an unknown one suggested that the unknown traffic came from the same family.

The speaker then presented a prototype HTTP fingerprinter that adds URL length, file extension, parameter count, header order and payload entropy features. Tests showed collisions where two families shared headers and differed only in URL. The closing message is that fingerprints stay useful until malware adapts, and that uniqueness must be balanced against generalization. The prototype is open source and invites issues and pull requests.

talks.title: 12. Yael Daihes - Mylobot, Detecting the Undetected with Deep Learning
talks.teaser: Shows how a deep learning model spots domain generation algorithm traffic in DNS data and tracks the Mylobot botnet's variants.
talks.summary:
The talk examines Mylobot, a botnet whose malware uses a domain generation algorithm (DGA) to produce long lists of random-looking domains and choose one for command and control each day. Blocking single domains does little, and reversing a sample only helps when the seed can be recovered. The speaker explains why earlier heuristics based on character frequency failed once attackers made generated names resemble ordinary domains.

The presenter describes a deep learning detector built on an LSTM sequence model, trained on DGA and benign domains, which reached above 90 percent accuracy in tests but could not say which malware family produced a domain. To attribute traffic, the system groups domains queried by one client in a short window, scores each one, then clusters the flagged groups by the pattern they share. In production this flags about 2.5 million domains a day and tracks roughly eight unnamed DGA groups, with near-zero false positives reported.

Applied to Mylobot, the system found about four variants with different name patterns, while public reports had covered only one. Pivoting through VirusTotal showed shared IP addresses across variants and sinkholing activity on some of them. Query volume reportedly grew to about 200 million DNS requests a day, and infected entities roughly doubled over the year. The takeaway is that network-level DNS monitoring can detect and block DGA traffic and support threat intelligence without endpoint access.

talks.title: 4. Bartosz Jerzman - AFT in action (African Financial Threats)
talks.teaser: Surveys African bank-focused crime groups, their insider laptop kill chain, and ways to cluster Python keyloggers and GrubZone C2.
talks.summary:
The session positions African financial threats as a distinct problem for global banks with presence in the region. Attacks rarely begin with remote spearphishing; instead, bribed or disgruntled insiders attach dedicated Windows laptops running commercial remote-access products. Operators then reconnoiter the network, move laterally with familiar tooling, and rely heavily on Python keyloggers compiled with PyInstaller rather than on password dumping alone. Cash-out phases pair broad internal access with insider help opening accounts and distributing ATM cards to large networks of money mules.

The middle of the talk maps East African groups from the Forkbombo cartel through post-arrest splinters such as Silentcards, the Consultants, and GrubZone, including tool choices, fast operational tempo, and obstacles defenders face when local corruption supports criminals. West African links such as OPERA and cooperation with TA505 appear briefly. The first case study compares keylogger families, showing reused functions, filenames tied to victim usernames, simple registry persistence, and hunting hints such as stray files under ProgramData.

The second case study examines 2020 GrubZone infrastructure around a single public IP using Shodan history, possible RDP tunneling tied to the National Bank of Kenya, the HR Shell Python backdoor, rare HTTP redirect behavior on the commander path, SSL and response-body pivots, and manifest-based sample discovery. The speaker stresses confidence labeling when infrastructure is shared hosting, and closes by urging proactive hunting where hardware-assisted initial access may already be inside the network.

talks.title: 6. Noa Weiss - The Unspoken Problems With Machine Learning in Security
talks.teaser: Explains why machine learning lags in security, from anomaly detection false positives to scarce labeled data and explainability.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that machine learning in security trails other fields, and it starts by showing where computer vision and natural language processing have reached. The examples include image completion, photos generated from rough sketches, synthetic faces, a language model that writes code and handles a coding interview, and a phone-booking assistant. In security, the speaker points to malware detection as a clear gain, while noting that most security models perform modestly and make up only a small part of products.

Anomaly detection is the most common approach in security because it fits the business need and does not require labeled data. It produces many false positives, though, and reviewing them costs analyst time and adds delay. The speaker also describes further obstacles: an environment of devices, applications and protocols that keeps changing, adversaries who adapt to evade models, scarce expert-labeled data, heavily imbalanced classes where the malicious cases are rare, and a strong need for explainability that deep learning models struggle to provide.

Confidentiality keeps most security data private, so there are few public, current datasets for benchmarking new methods. The speaker's suggested path forward is direct collaboration between security companies to build and share public datasets, which would enable common benchmarks and more open discussion. The talk presents these as the speaker's own suggestions and opinions, and it invites audience feedback afterwards.

talks.title: 1. Vitali Kremez - Hidden Link Between TrickBot Anchor & North Korea Lazarus State Sponsored Group
talks.teaser: Connects the Anchor malware, a TrickBot offshoot, to North Korea's Lazarus group and shows crypto-routine YARA hunting.
talks.summary:
Vitali Kremez presents research that ties the crimeware group behind TrickBot to North Korean state-linked activity. He describes how financially motivated crews have shifted toward high-value targets, using reconnaissance of network and Active Directory records from infected machines, then deploying ransomware or handing access to skilled operators who use penetration testing frameworks such as Cobalt Strike and PowerShell Empire. The focus is Anchor, a TrickBot-derived project built for selective intrusions.

The connection surfaced while hunting for TrickBot crypters. An Anchor sample's PDB path led the team to a server whose task command downloaded and executed PowerShell tools attributed to Lazarus. The same execution pattern appeared in an intrusion at a Chilean bank, where a developer ran a binary delivered through a fake Skype job interview. The talk also covers the Bangladesh Bank heist, the use of casinos to cash out stolen funds, and the related North Korean groups APT38 and APT37.

For defenders, Kremez shows YARA rules that target cryptographic routines instead of plain strings. One example is a modified RC4 implementation with a changed S-box and a null terminator in the key, which helped link samples across operations. His takeaway is that analysts should study attacker behavior closely and treat crimeware activity as a possible route to state-linked actors.

talks.title: 7. Allie Mellen - Trust, but Verify: Maintaining Democracy In Spite of Информационные контрмеры
talks.teaser: Maps election interference across infrastructure, information, and ethos layers and urges broader defenses beyond voting machines alone.
talks.summary:
Federal and state election work often focuses on voter rolls and voting equipment, while much of what shapes whether people vote sits outside that narrow IT boundary. The presentation frames participation through Maslow’s hierarchy and a parallel “voter hierarchy of needs,” arguing that fear for safety, belonging, esteem, and belief that a ballot matters can suppress turnout as surely as tampering with machines. In the United States, roughly forty percent of eligible citizens do not vote, so even small friction across those needs can shift outcomes.

From an attacker mindset aligned with red-team practice, nation states typically pursue power, ideology, and global standing by striking three planes: infrastructure, information, and ethos. Historical and modern cases span Italian Cold War propaganda, foreign funding scandals, 2016 social and text-based deceptions, compromise and DDoS against Ukraine’s election commission, false polling-location messages, assassinations and purges that shatter trust, Estonia’s 2007 riots paired with banking and media denial of service, grid outages, and ransomware on transit systems that block the trip to polls after work.

Defenders are urged to widen “election security” to communications, social platforms, transit, and power, recognize private-sector systems as part of the attack surface, build government partnerships with clear points of contact, and respond to misinformation by reporting it and addressing trusted contacts with facts rather than amplifying false narratives.

talks.title: 14. Grzegorz Tworek - The Good, the Bad and the ETW
talks.teaser: Walks through Windows monitoring options and Event Tracing for Windows, with live demos of providers, sessions and trace collection.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Grzegorz Tworek (also introducing himself as Greg), Malware Security Lead Engineer at Standard Chartered, provides a practical crash course on Windows monitoring mechanisms with a primary focus on Event Tracing for Windows (ETW). Aimed at blue teamers, red teamers, system administrators, and developers, the talk surveys built-in Windows telemetry options before diving into the architecture, security configurations, sniffing opportunities, and evasion or triggering techniques associated with ETW.

### Key Topics
- **Windows Monitoring Landscape**: A comparison of various built-in diagnostic and monitoring facilities, including classic Event Logs, Performance Counters, debug output (monitored via Sysinternals DebugView), Windows Software Trace Preprocessor (WPP), In-Flight Trace Recorder (IFR) kept in circular memory dumps, and kernel black boxes for boot and services.
- **ETW Architecture**: Introduction to the core ETW engine, introduced in Windows Vista, which connects controllers, event providers, and consumers, with support for live sessions (`-ets`) and binary event trace log (`.etl`) files.
- **Provider Management and Manifests**: Inspecting and discovering providers using native command-line utilities (`logman query providers`) and registry keys (`HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\WMI\Security` and Autologgers). Demonstrating manifest extraction from binary hard links using Resource Hacker to view `WEVT_TEMPLATE` resources.
- **Access Control & Permissions**: Analyzing security descriptors in the registry and utilizing PowerShell to parse provider ACLs and SDDL strings to see which accounts (Local System, Administrators, Authenticated Users) can read or write events.
- **Blinding & Evasion**: Demonstrating how unregistering providers, tampering with Autologger registry values (`Enable`), or setting the environment variable `COMPlus_ETWEnabled=0` disables .NET ETW telemetry inside processes.

### Technical Details
- **Native CLI Commands**: Tworek relies heavily on built-in tools like `logman` (e.g., `logman query -ets`, `logman start osk -p "Microsoft-Windows-OSK" -o osk.etl -ets`, `logman stop osk -ets`) and `tracerpt` (e.g., `tracerpt osk.etl -o osk.xml`) to collect and convert traces without third-party dependencies.
- **Sniffing with ETW**: The speaker highlights sensitive telemetry that ETW providers capture, including cleartext HTTP/HTTPS data via `WinINet` before TLS encapsulation, network frames via built-in packet providers, USB bus traffic, and on-screen keyboard keystrokes via `Microsoft-Windows-OSK`. Tworek demonstrates sniffing OSK inputs, extracting `tcID` values from the resulting XML trace, and mapping those decimal scan codes to raw keyboard inputs.
- **Service Triggering via ETW**: Demonstrating that while an unprivileged regular user receives an `error 5` (access denied) when attempting to start a service such as the Windows Error Reporting Service (`WerSvc`), the service configuration has an ETW event trigger (`sc qtriggerinfo WerSvc`). By calling the undocumented `ntdll.dll` export `EtwEventWriteNoRegistration`, an unprivileged user can emit the trigger event and cause the Service Control Manager to start the target service.
- **Ecosystem Tools**: Recommending utilities such as Microsoft Message Analyzer, TraceView (SDK/WDK), FireEye's SilkETW, Pavel Yosifovich's ETW Explorer, Zac Brown's Posh-ETW, and Airbus CERT's WinShark.

### Takeaways
ETW provides an extremely powerful, low-overhead monitoring architecture with over a thousand native providers, but its security implications cut both ways. Administrators and defenders must recognize that ETW can expose sensitive cleartext data (keystrokes, network frames, decrypted web traffic), can be blinded via registry manipulation or environment variables, and can even be abused by unprivileged users to indirectly execute actions such as triggering service starts.

talks.title: 17. Jake Kamieniak
talks.teaser: Explains how red teams decide what to keep secret from defenders, and how to make those opsec choices transparent.
talks.summary:
Jake Kamieniak, a red teamer on an internal company team, treats operational security, or opsec, as a process for protecting the information that would most hurt a mission if an adversary obtained it. Red teams routinely keep targets, timing and techniques from defenders, and that secrecy can make blue teams feel distrusted. The talk asks when such secrecy is justified and how to manage it.

Three disclosure decisions are examined. For vulnerabilities, the question is whether reporting one would expose second-order details such as where the team operates or how its command-and-control infrastructure is built. For techniques, exact command syntax helps defenders write detections that block only the red team, so sharing the general technology area is preferred. For access, a web flaw is a single fixable issue, while a phishing path reflects layered failures and can recur after cleanup.

The closing argument is that opsec should serve the red team's strategy, which should fit in a sentence or two. The speaker's team aims to prepare the company for an inevitable breach by realistically simulating an APT and sparring with blue. Secrets need a reason and an explanation to peers, and recording opsec decisions in a living document helps keep trust intact.

talks.title: 8. Robert Sell - The Art of the Breach
talks.teaser: Maps attacker reconnaissance, pretexts, and forced-entry tools from the sidewalk through the building to the executive filing cabinet.
talks.summary:
The session frames a full physical intrusion path defenders should expect, from pre-operation homework through escape. It opens by arguing that many physical-security talks stop short of a end-to-end breach, then promises a sidewalk-to-filing-cabinet journey that blends passive reconnaissance, social engineering, covert entry, and forced entry.

The homework phase treats open-source intelligence as zero-touch reconnaissance: dedicated VMs, sock puppets, VPN use, and organized note-taking. The speaker stresses understanding the target’s business, employee oversharing, vendors for pretexts, floor plans, ingress and egress, magnetic locks, guards, CCTV, patterns of life, and YouTube office tours. On site, research is verified before choosing front versus back doors, cloning risks at card readers, lobby and hallway movement, elevators and stairs, and executive areas.

Forced-entry tooling gets concrete treatment—wedges, cutters, modified pliers, shove knives, crowbars, hinge attacks, padlocks, first-responder key boxes, and filing-cabinet weaknesses—along with timing estimates for breaching typical steel and layered rear doors. The close shifts to defender takeaways: perimeter walks, tamper alarms on readers, limiting Knox-box scope, stairwell cameras, and realistic expectations about guards, CCTV, and exfiltration tricks such as crowds and fire alarms.

talks.title: 9. Joe Slowik
talks.teaser: Explores how attackers exploit process and supplier dependencies to cause outsized disruption, and how defenders can map them.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a 2019 drone and missile strike on a Saudi oil and gas processing facility, arguing that hitting one critical node can halt an entire industry. The speaker places that event alongside disruptive malware campaigns against Gulf energy firms and presents cyber as one means to an attacker's goal. Process complexity, just-in-time production, supplier reliance and cloud dependence all create points whose loss cascades outward.

Several historical cases follow. In 2014, intrusions around Ukraine's presidential election aimed to block official results, and the media was an external dependency that could amplify fake figures beyond the defenders' control. In 2015, an attack on Ukrainian electric distribution went past the outage to disable communication converters, uninterruptible power supplies and operator workstations, though operators restored power by moving to manual control. In 2016, a second Ukrainian grid attack used a denial of service against a digital protective relay so that restored lines would run unprotected. Triton malware in a Saudi oil and gas plant was meant to alter safety systems but instead caused a safety trip. A 2018 intrusion into a pipeline data and billing system impaired operations, and late 2019 ransomware on a pipeline operator's IT forced a shutdown without touching the pipeline itself.

The practical takeaway is to defend what the organization values, not only its networks. Defenders should identify value-generating processes and their critical nodes, map the IT systems that support them, and confirm visibility into those assets. Resiliency means restoring data and configurations to a known-good state, not just rebuilding machines. Tabletop exercises and purple-team style scenarios that include operations staff and third-party providers can expose gaps before an adversary finds them.

talks.title: 16. Josh Miller - CyberSafari: Underexamined threat actors from the global threat landscape
talks.teaser: Surveys lesser-known state-linked threat actors across regions, covering their targets, methods and attribution clues.
talks.summary:
Josh Miller presents a tour of state-linked intrusion groups that receive less attention than the most widely reported ones. He explains that he leaves out the usual large actors and the Five Eyes countries, then sets out a framework for thinking about adversaries. The Diamond model is used to organise infrastructure, victims, capabilities and the adversary, and a scale of national responsibility runs from states that prosecute third-party hackers to states that run operations with their own forces.

The middle of the talk covers regional cases. A 2018 newspaper report described Dutch operators reaching APT29's network and recording people entering its building, which helped tie the group to the SVR. Turkey-linked Sea Turtle carried out DNS hijacking against national security organisations in the Middle East and North Africa. Lebanon's Dark Karakol relied on mobile malware, and exposed logs led investigators to Wi-Fi networks near a government official's building. Pakistan-linked Gorgon Group used URL shortening services to deliver payloads, and India-linked Patchwork reused an exploit taken from a public GitHub proof-of-concept. Vietnam's APT32 targeted foreign manufacturers as car import rules changed.

The talk closes with trends. Smaller governments are using targeted intrusions against dissidents, journalists and sometimes their own citizens. Miller suggests that multinational companies threat model the governments that affect their local subsidiaries, read reporting from regional vendors, and adopt stronger account protection such as hardware tokens. Red teams can use the same tradecraft to look more like real adversaries.

talks.title: 12. x33fcon 2019 - Attacking AWS: the full cyber kill chain by Paweł Rzepa
talks.teaser: Shows a live AWS attack chain, from SSRF and instance metadata to admin access and hidden CloudTrail changes.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through a hypothetical attack on a company running fully on AWS, shown as a live demo of a complete kill chain. It starts with cloud-specific reconnaissance, such as matching an address to the public AWS IP ranges to see which service hosts it. A server-side request forgery flaw in a web application then reaches the instance metadata service and returns the credentials of the instance role.

Using the Pacu framework, the attacker enumerates the role's permissions, finds a wildcard policy allowing any EC2 action, and locates a stopped test instance with an admin profile. Rewriting that instance's user data to open a reverse shell on its next start yields admin credentials. The talk then covers hiding activity: a CloudTrail trail can be switched to a single region or disabled, a billing alarm removed, and extra access keys added to existing users, which GuardDuty did not flag.

The speaker lists what went wrong: an exposed application, an admin-level test instance, missing monitoring and misconfigured services. The blocked IP address in the reported case was bypassed by using decimal or hexadecimal forms. Recommended assessments combine architecture review, configuration checks against the CIS benchmark with Prowler, penetration testing and verification of monitoring, and a Gartner estimate is cited that through 2022 at least 95% of cloud security failures would be customers' fault.

talks.title: 11. x33fcon 2019 - SS7 for INFOSEC by Paul Coggin
talks.teaser: Explains how attackers could reach SS7 signalling networks through vendor backdoors and abandoned equipment.
talks.summary:
Paul Coggin opens by asking how an attacker would get a first foothold into SS7 networks, which are normally closed. He explains SS7 as the signalling system carriers use to route calls and messages, and compares its trust model to BGP on the internet. He walks through core elements such as signal transfer points, service control points, and the home and visitor location registers that track mobile subscribers.

The middle of the talk centres on access paths. Coggin describes vendor remote access that bypasses corporate controls, such as Linux boxes multi-homed into management networks with open SSH, and a carrier migration where abandoned routers kept their passwords and SNMP community strings. Once inside, he outlines how an attacker could impersonate a switch to query a subscriber's location, then manipulate location updates to redirect or intercept calls and texts. He notes that some features, such as the anytime interrogation feature, are being locked down, though many networks remain unpatched.

He closes with advice for auditors: legacy systems may crash under malformed packets, so testing needs care. He suggests reconsidering SMS-based two-factor authentication, since he showed SMS can be targeted through these paths, and urges consultants to look at network visibility such as NetFlow and centralized logging, which he says is often neglected in voice networks.

talks.title: 10. x33fcon 2019 - Hunters ATT&CKing with the right data! by Roberto Rodriguez Jose Louis Rodriguez
talks.teaser: Shows how mapping logs to MITRE ATT&CK data sources helps hunters know which events really prove a technique.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that threat hunting depends on knowing what security data actually means before any analytics are built. The speakers say many organisations collect logs but cannot describe what each event contains, and that a single ATT&CK data source such as Windows event logs can cover hundreds of distinct events. They present a method for mapping event logs to ATT&CK data sources, using data dictionaries that record field names, types and meanings, and a data model that links entities such as users, processes and IP addresses.

Using the ATT&CK data pulled from its public TAXII server, they report that almost half of the roughly 485 techniques have data sources. Process monitoring relates to 169 of 240 techniques, but only 21 can be validated with one data source, while 219 need at least two. A live overpass-the-hash demo compared Mimikatz and Rubeus: Rubeus avoids LSASS and creates a sacrificial logon session with random strings, while Sysmon shows the user and the connection to port 88 that Windows event 5156 does not provide.

The takeaway for practitioners is to identify which events confirm a specific behaviour, such as a WMI parent process making a network connection, rather than relying on a data source name alone. The speakers also pointed to the Mordor project of pre-recorded event datasets and said an APT3 dataset would be released.

talks.title: 09. x33fcon 2019
talks.teaser: Shows statistical and header-based methods for spotting C2 beaconing in HTTP logs, plus fake TLS detection.
talks.summary:
This talk covers hunting beaconing, the periodic check-ins malware makes to its command-and-control server, mostly using HTTP logs from a NATO cyber defense exercise. Signatures rarely catch well-configured beacons, so the speaker tests behavioural hypotheses instead. The first measures how regular connection intervals are, using the coefficient of variation to separate automated jittered beacons from manually paced sessions. The same method surfaces slow beacons that check in about every half hour.

The next hypotheses focus on HTTP metadata. Grouping requests by URI across hosts can reveal backup C2 domains sharing one path. A single destination receiving many different URIs with an unchanged referrer suggests automation, because browsers normally update the referrer as users navigate. Constant URI length can flag encoded payloads stored in the path.

The talk then turns to a fake TLS protocol linked to the Lazarus group, where the handshake imitates a legitimate site but the real traffic afterward uses a pre-shared key. The early message sizes are fixed and too small to be genuine TLS records, which makes them a profiling target for network analysts and sandbox captures. The closing section shows how to find C2 servers through default Cobalt Strike behaviour, such as its team server management port, DNS listener replies and HTTP server quirks, and urges defenders to hunt for defaults and operator mistakes.

talks.title: 07. x33fcon 2019 - Techniques and Tools for becoming an Intelligence Operator by Robert Sell
talks.teaser: Practitioners learn operational security, collection tooling, and pivot techniques drawn from Trace Labs missing-person searches.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames intelligence work around Trace Labs, a nonprofit that runs conference and school OSINT events to help law enforcement locate real missing people. It explains why the group stays passive—no friending, messaging, or direct contact—and only acts when agencies publicly ask for help, across cases such as people hiding from obligations, trafficking victims, and abductions.

Much of the session is a practitioner playbook: operational security before engaging risky subjects, scoping objectives and deliverables, and building a reusable lab with virtual machines, common frameworks, evidence capture, and VPN use. It walks through target acquisition (identifiers, mobility, sophistication, and peripheral pivots via friends, employers, sports, forums, and fitness apps), then concrete collection paths for real names, usernames, email verification and breach correlation, Snapchat and map-based geolocation, archived social content, Google Street View timelines, travel platforms, and physical versus technical infrastructure for people and companies.

Three Trace Labs cases show how small forum or lifestyle clues chain into usernames, associates, and risk context, including situations where subjects vanish online entirely. The close covers evasion habits, possible honeypot-style awareness traps, growing law-enforcement adoption of crowdsourced intel, and ethical tension as low-cost profiling becomes routine—plus books, podcasts, and ways to join ongoing operations.

talks.title: 06. x33fcon 2019 - Atomic Threat Coverage: How to ATT&CK by Danil Yugoslavsky & Mateusz Wydra
talks.teaser: Shows how to turn MITRE ATT&CK mappings into maintained detection rules, data requirements, and playbooks from plain-text files.
talks.summary:
The speakers, who work on SOC and threat detection teams, start from a practical problem: ATT&CK describes techniques at a high level, so turning them into detections, justifying log sources to engineers, and reporting progress to management takes a lot of manual research. Their earlier framework mapped ATT&CK techniques to alerts, required data, logging policies and response steps in a Confluence knowledge base, but unit tests, detection logic and page updates were still handled by hand, and changes rippled across many linked pages.

The replacement, Atomic Threat Coverage, keeps every entity in YAML files. It pulls in Sigma detection rules and Atomic Red Team tests, then generates Markdown or Confluence pages, HIVE case templates built from response playbooks, Kibana dashboards, and ATT&CK Navigator layers per customer. A live demo showed a detection page linking its ATT&CK mappings, generated queries for chosen SIEMs, the data needed and the logging policy that produces it. The dashboards showed that most of the 211 open-source Sigma rules were not yet implemented for the sample customer, and nearly 80 percent carried experimental status, so they need testing before production use.

The closing section covered the workflow: changes go through Git and merge requests, one make command regenerates all outputs, and the data stays compatible with community projects that can be pulled in directly. The speakers also outlined next steps, including a shared coverage definition, more ATT&CK-mapped projects such as Metasploit post-exploitation modules, and automated hardening driven by ATT&CK mappings.

talks.title: 04. x33fcon 2019 - Chaos in the Machine: APT28 Complex by Jason Kitchen & Alex Orleans
talks.teaser: Examines how internal politics, rivalry and national pride shape APT28 operations and the mistakes they produce.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that state-sponsored intrusions are not as orderly as their reputation suggests. The speakers, who draw on their experience tracking state actors, treat groups such as APT28 (fancy bear) and Sandworm as human organizations shaped by competing priorities, fear of exposure and internal politics. Their analysis rests on open-source reporting and two 2018 US government indictments of GRU officers, and they present the links between units and activity clusters as working assumptions.

They describe how chaos moves down from strategic culture, organizational culture, rivalry between intelligence agencies, leadership demands and domestic politics to the operators on keyboard. Case studies include the 2016 US election intrusions, where fancy bear and cozy bear were both inside the same party networks and were removed, showing a lack of deconfliction. Closed-access operations against anti-doping bodies were driven by a desire to recover national prestige, and they reused personnel and laptops despite high risk. An attempted closed-access operation against the OPCW was tracked and disrupted. The talk also contrasts these with a 2018 US Cyber Command action against the Internet Research Agency.

For practitioners, the takeaway is to treat attribution as input to detection and emulation rather than just a label. Teams can ask what data an actor would value given current events, include physical and radio-frequency exposure such as how far office Wi-Fi reaches in red team scope, and consider how institutional pressure affects an actor's tool choices and operational tradeoffs.

talks.title: 02. x33fcon 2019 - Out of the Blue by Marc Smeets & Mark Bergman
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning 02. x33fcon 2019 - Out of the Blue by Marc Smeets & Mark Bergman.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at x33fcon 2019, Marc Smeets and Mark Bergman discuss the concept of red teaming as a collaborative sparring match rather than an adversarial contest. They explain that the goal of a red team is to train and improve the defensive capabilities of the blue team. As red team operations expand across complex infrastructure—often encompassing dozens of redirectors and multiple command-and-control (C2) servers—operators face significant challenges maintaining operational oversight and insight. To address this, the speakers introduce two open-source tools: RedELK, an operational data collection and SIEM framework for red teams, and RedFile, a lightweight Python-based tool for dynamic, rule-based payload delivery.

### Key Topics
- **Philosophy of Red Teaming**: Comparing red teaming to boxing training, the speakers emphasize that an undetected operation is a failure because it denies the blue team an opportunity to learn. Red teaming should focus on engagement, training, and reaching actual business crown jewels rather than simply achieving domain admin privileges.
- **Operational Scale and Complexity**: Realistic offensive operations often scale to 40–50 systems, including 4–5 backend C2 servers and 15–20 redirectors across multiple concurrent scenarios. Operators require centralized management to track who is scanning, interacting with, or analyzing their infrastructure.
- **Locard's Exchange Principle Applied to Cyber Operations**: Citing Edmond Locard's principle that "every contact leaves a trace," the speakers note that while red teams leave traces for blue teams to find, blue team investigations, online sandboxes, and automated scanners also leave detectable traces for red teams.
- **Centralized Telemetry with RedELK**: Combining the ELK stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, and Kibana) with Filebeat, RedELK aggregates web traffic logs from front-end redirectors (such as HAProxy) and operational logs from C2 platforms like Cobalt Strike into a unified interface.
- **Dynamic Payload Delivery with RedFile**: A modular Python tool deployed on web servers that dynamically serves payloads or decoy content based on request attributes such as IP addresses, user agents, frequency, or request sequence.

### Technical Details
- **RedELK Architecture**: RedELK uses Filebeat agents deployed on first-line redirectors and C2 team servers to ingest traffic and operational logs into Logstash, enrich the data, and index it into Elasticsearch with a tailored Kibana front end. It periodically copies screenshots, keystrokes, and downloaded files from C2 servers to a central repository.
- **Supported Platforms & Integrations**: RedELK natively supports Cobalt Strike out of the box without requiring custom CNA scripts, with planned future support for Faction C2 and Empire. For redirection, initial support centers on HAProxy, with upcoming support for Nginx and Apache.
- **Data Enrichment & Periodic Tasks**: RedELK runs background tasks that execute every minute to tag IP addresses (categorizing them as belonging to the red team, the customer, or unknown entities via GeoIP and IP whitelists). Every two minutes, operational files are synchronized from team servers. Every five minutes, rule-based alarms run to detect anomalies, such as an internal IOC appearing on external security providers (VirusTotal, IBM X-Force, hybrid analysis) or unexpected IP addresses interacting with C2 endpoints.
- **Defensive Artifacts and Investigation Traces**: The speakers demonstrate how EDR solutions (such as Symantec EDR and Microsoft Defender ATP) allow analysts to submit samples to cloud sandboxes with a single click. These sandbox detonations trigger live call-backs with distinctive, identifiable computer names and behavior patterns, followed hours later by broader waves of automated multi-sandbox and vendor scanners (e.g., Trustwave).
- **RedFile Capabilities**: RedFile enables dynamic file serving in very few lines of Python code. Demonstrated use cases include restricting payloads by IP whitelists, rate-limiting payload delivery (e.g., serving a payload only once every 30 seconds to prevent runaway migrations caused by a user opening multiple documents), and sequentially changing responses per URL (e.g., returning robots.txt on the first click, a fake bitcoin stealer on the second, and a rickroll video on subsequent clicks to mislead defensive investigations).

### Takeaways
- Centralizing red team operational data into a dedicated SIEM like RedELK provides situational awareness, enables swift reporting of IOCs and operator commands to the client, and monitors when defenders detect offensive infrastructure.
- Defensive actions and EDR sandboxes inadvertently signal their activities back to red teams by querying online threat intelligence platforms and generating automated analysis traffic.
- Pairing passive monitoring (RedELK) with active, dynamic file delivery (RedFile) empowers red teams to tailor their activities in real time to match the blue team's training needs.

talks.title: 01. x33fcon 2019
talks.teaser: Shows how threat intelligence and red and blue teams can work together against state-linked threat actors.
talks.summary:
The talk challenges the idea that red and blue teams are opposing sides, arguing that defenders need both mindsets and a shared language. The speaker, who has spent about 20 years on threat hunting, presents a target-centric methodology in which intelligence matters only if the consuming team can act on it. He argues defenders should focus on how attacks happen more than on who carried them out.

To make the point he walks through state-linked espionage using public US Department of Justice indictments of China-linked operators. He shows that threat groups are fluid, that members can be added or swapped, and that insiders were co-opted to report on incident response and plant malware. Mapping the observed techniques onto delivery categories such as phishing, web compromise, human-enabled access and supply chain attacks, he notes that insider co-option rarely appears in attack models. He also outlines a ten-question framework applied to each capability, with a PowerShell study that produced 67 pages of raw material.

On the red team side he presents the team as collector, advocate and educator, and warns against blame culture and against writing IOC-specific detections aimed at red teamers. He compares adversary breakout time and a cited 101-day dwell time to judge whether a defender's process can keep pace. He closes by urging teams to assess coverage across endpoint, network, identity, application and data, and to close gaps between red and blue against a shared threat.

talks.summary:
In this short interview clip from x33fcon 2024, Bart Inglot introduces his upcoming session, Attack Antics. He explains that the session picks out some of the more interesting techniques his team has seen attackers use and presents nine of them in about 45 minutes. The techniques were chosen because they were not tied to a single client; similar behaviour turned up in various environments.

The main point he wants audiences to take away is that attackers work at different levels and adapt to the environment they land in, so defenders need a holistic view. He stresses staying agile, learning about different attacker methods, and then checking whether those behaviours are present in your own environment. He also describes a common pattern in which blue and red teams do not trust each other, or an organisation hires consultants who return six months later with exactly the same findings, and he argues that defenders must adapt and actually address the issues.

Discussing the market in Asia, he says maturity is lower there, which leaves plenty of room for growth. He notes cases dating back ten years that clients still struggle to remediate, and says it is not easy for organisations to fully remove every threat actor that might be in their environments.

talks.title: 09. x33fcon 2018 - Advances in IPv6 Network Reconnaissance by Fernando Gont
talks.teaser: Covers practical IPv6 reconnaissance: search engines, certificate logs, DNS walking, and lessons learned from field measurements.
talks.summary:
Fernando Gont reviews recent progress in IPv6 network reconnaissance. Sweeping every address fails at IPv6 scale, so the talk focuses on methods that shrink the search space. One is harvesting domain names from search engines for a DNS zone. Google results proved obfuscated, while another engine tolerated heavy querying; varying the query with a keyword dictionary surfaced many new names.

Certificate transparency logs form a complementary source, since they list names that received certificates even when no website uses them. Address patterns matter too. Newer standards replaced MAC-derived interface identifiers with randomized ones, and measurements of popular-site lists showed most addresses still embedding IPv4 addresses, plus a larger random share that pattern scanners cannot target. Reverse DNS walking via ip6.arpa is another option, but wildcard records inflate results, and prefixes of /48 or smaller worked more reliably.

The talk closed with a prototype that merges these sources and a Q&A on whether randomized addresses reveal operating systems, which had not been tested. Practitioners should combine several sources, filter wildcard noise, and split large prefixes.

talks.title: 08. Joe Slowik interview
talks.teaser: Behavioral threat attribution prioritizes adversary actions over actor labels to shape defenses and purple-team exercises.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens with brief remarks about the host conference in Poland as a venue that blends offensive and defensive audiences. The substantive thread is threat attribution in intelligence work, which often fixates on naming states or entities as culprits. The speaker argues for shifting emphasis to behavior: how activity unfolded, what techniques were used, and which observables defenders can rely on instead of debating identity alone.

That framing is tied to red and blue collaboration. Red personnel gain a clearer mandate to emulate realistic adversary actions rather than play-act a specific national profile. Blue teams can align monitoring, controls, and response playbooks to those behaviors, which the speaker presents as a way to prioritize scarce defensive effort and reduce bias when guessing what a motivated attacker would do against a given target.

The closing argument is that purple teaming is not optional if defenses are to improve without waiting for real incidents. Plans need continuous adversarial testing. The speaker contrasts large events that skew heavily red or heavily blue with conferences designed to force ongoing interaction, suggesting that model as a practical path for maturing both sides.

talks.title: 06. x33fcon 2018 - Death by a Thousand Struts: A Defenders Tale by sixdub
talks.teaser: A defender shows how default Struts IDS signatures miss alternate gadgets and how behavioral network rules close the gap.
talks.summary:
The presenter describes moving between offensive and defensive roles and how that background helped during incident response involving Cobalt Strike and repeated Apache Struts cases after the 2017 disclosure wave. He explains why Struts remained a high-value internet-facing target, cites ongoing scanning behavior, and groups real outcomes into opportunistic automated compromise, enterprise ransomware that began with an external Struts flaw, and slower targeted data theft long after patches existed.

Using public exploit material and a Suricata plus ELK setup, he first shows a successful default exploit and matching emerging-threat alerts, then dissects why those rules only cover specific Java gadgets, ysoserial usage, and fixed plugin paths. A second demonstration with marshal SEC and a remote class-loader payload achieves command execution without triggering the stock rules. He proposes a practitioner workflow—adversary technique selection, intelligence gathering, strict versus loose detection criteria for POSTed XML abuse, overlapping indicators, durability testing, and maintenance—and sketches behavioral hunts such as non-browser TLS fingerprints, rare external URIs, inbound POST paired with outbound callbacks, and correlation with endpoint process creation.

He closes by arguing red teams should exercise detection and response across the kill chain with explicit training goals, including willingness to run noisy exploits when that is the learning objective, plus atomic detection testing and sustained purple-team collaboration so organizations improve after engagements rather than treating a single alert as victory.

talks.title: 04. x33fcon 2018 - This is enterprise grade solution - and that is how we root it ;) by keidii
talks.teaser: A researcher explains how curiosity and missteps exposed root-level flaws across a bundled enterprise web and email security suite.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that enterprise-grade security bundles can create a false sense of safety while remaining as bug-prone as any other software. The presenter did not run a formal penetration test; instead, day-to-day bank operations, proxy misconfiguration, and odd support requests led into a Forcepoint-style websense stack spanning email gateway, HTTP proxy, Triton administration, and PAM quarantine review.

Reported issues span trivial admin input handling, HTML rendering of mail already labeled malicious (including self-release and injection paths), localhost requests steered through the corporate proxy to exposed appliance HTTP on high ports with root-backed configuration, JSP smuggling via CID attachment rendering, and a repeatable segmentation fault in an HP mwx document parser used for DLP—minimized to an oversized image description in a Word file and turned into straightforward remote code execution as root on the mail path. The speaker also criticizes a drawn-out vendor disclosure timeline on version 8.1 while production still carried serious remote-root exposure.

Takeaways stress defense in depth inside the product itself: never run components as root, never execute untrusted quarantine content as full HTML, do not ignore crashes (here crashes could mark mail clean), constrain localhost APIs, and operate transparent bug-reporting programs with clear status for researchers.

talks.title: 03. x33fcon 2018 - Threat-based Purple Teaming with ATT&CK by Chris and Cody from MITRE
talks.teaser: Shows how red and blue teams can use MITRE ATT&CK and adversary emulation plans to run iterative purple team exercises.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the usual split between red and blue teams, where red reports may hold back details and blue teams struggle to test new detections afterwards. The speakers argue for purple teaming, in which both sides work together and share a common language. They present MITRE ATT&CK as that shared vocabulary, organizing adversary behaviors into tactics and techniques and favoring behaviors over easily changed indicators such as hashes or IP addresses.

Adversary emulation is framed as threat-based red teaming: a specific actor's techniques are scoped against time, resources and threat intelligence. The worked example is an APT3 plan built from open-source reporting in three phases, with each implant function mapped to ATT&CK and carried out with Windows built-in tools, Cobalt Strike or Metasploit. They advise stripping default framework settings that make traffic easy to signature, and marking each technique on a matrix as undetected, partly visible or detected.

The main takeaway is that iterative sessions, where red and blue walk through each technique together, lead to faster fixes and reusable playbooks. The APT3 plan was released publicly, an APT29 plan was still under review, and the ATT&CK Navigator helps visualize coverage. In questions, they pointed to open projects such as Atomic Red Team and Caldera for detailed detection guidance, and invited community contributions.

talks.title: 02. x33fcon 2018
talks.teaser: Walks through reusable open-source pentest documents and engagement types, from opportunistic attacks to stolen-laptop scenarios.
talks.summary:
The speaker presents an open-source set of penetration testing and red team documentation, built because every employer ran tests differently and paperwork was rebuilt each time. The templates cover an NDA with vulnerability disclosure terms, a trimmed statement of work, rules of engagement, and a deliverables request that ties the client's inputs to deadlines. A communication agreement sets how often the parties talk and what happens after unscheduled outages or intrusions detected during a test. Clients are called partners, and a scoring rubric is shared with the blue team before testing starts.

The middle of the talk covers engagement types. An opportunistic attacker test runs loud, widely known tools across the network to see whether defenders notice. External testing with credentials checks whether logins reach code execution or corporate data, with an Outlook rule abused through email as one example. A stolen laptop or phone scenario asks whether lost devices, certificates and VPN access get revoked. Other scenarios include breach simulation, insider, physical and wireless work, plus egress testing, where a binary tests every outbound port over HTTP and produces a report.

Detection lessons close the talk. A rogue device left in a conference room stayed active for months, and C2 channels over HTTP, DNS, Twitter and Dropbox were caught while an old IRC bot got through. Adversarial simulation can also reveal when a log feed, such as a SIEM connector, goes quiet and silently stops detections. The templates are offered as a starting point, with a web app planned to combine them.

talks.title: 02. mubix (aka Rob Fuller) interview
talks.teaser: A short interview covers open-source pen testing practice, clearer engagement types, and sharing how teams work with customers.
talks.summary:
The speaker reflects on a conference presentation focused on open-source penetration testing and the friction practitioners face when every organization maintains its own documentation and engagement models. Starting a new role or firm means rebuilding that material from scratch, so he argues for standardization that helps customers and partners ask for specific outcomes rather than a vague pen test request.

He contrasts broad engagement labels with more defined work such as adversarial simulation or detection collaboration, and emphasizes sharing operational detail—not only exploit techniques but how engagements are scoped, delivered, and communicated. Red team and pen test staff are rarely documentation specialists, so widely reused models could reduce duplicated effort across the field.

He closes by noting that security maturity varies enormously across millions of organizations, which makes one-size-fits-all generalization unrealistic. Shared cloud services may raise baseline security for many tenants while introducing new exposure, so overall progress tends to be gradual rather than uniform.

talks.title: 14. Weaponizing the USB Armory by Yashin Mehaboobe
talks.teaser: Shows how a USB Armory board can act as a keystroke-injection and composite USB attack device.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at turning the USB Armory, a small Linux board in a USB stick form factor, into an offensive device for human interface device (HID) attacks. It explains why keyboard and mouse injection is often overlooked: a device that presents itself as a keyboard can type commands on a locked-down machine with no network exploit needed. Endpoint policies that block USB storage may not catch composite devices that combine several USB functions. The talk compares the board with earlier tools such as the Teensy, Rubber Ducky and Bash Bunny, and notes that running Linux on the Armory makes it easier to customise.

The demos use an open-source framework that generates payload scripts for a chosen target. The first shows a keystroke attack on Windows that opens the run prompt, types a command and launches PowerShell. The second uses a composite Ethernet and HID device with a DHCP server on the board, so injected commands can move data out over the network with netcat. Other options covered include a mass storage variant, a rogue SMB server approach that works against locked machines, and a idea of using a PIR sensor on the GPIO pins to check whether someone is present before running a payload. Composite support was unreliable on Windows 10, and HID work needed a 4.4 kernel image.

The main takeaway is that brief physical access with a plausible USB device can lead to command execution and data theft, so defenders should review USB policies for composite devices as well as storage. The speaker notes that documentation for the board is sparse and points to the vendor's community forum and kernel build examples for help.

talks.title: 13. Invoke-CradleCrafter: Moar PowerShell obFUsk8tion by Daniel Bohannon
talks.teaser: Introduces Invoke-CradleCrafter for building obfuscated PowerShell download cradles and lists behaviors defenders can monitor.
talks.summary:
Daniel Bohannon opens by explaining why download-and-execute cradles remain a focus after his earlier Invoke-Obfuscation work. He argues blocking PowerShell broadly is unrealistic because renamed binaries and post-execution abuse differ from the macro and initial-access problems defenders should prioritize first. He urges PowerShell 5 script block logging and references community detection work, including frequency analysis approaches applied to obfuscated output.

The core of the session is Invoke-CradleCrafter, released during the talk as a living catalog of cryptic cradle syntax. He groups cradles by disk, memory, and hybrid patterns, including BITs transfers that can work under constrained language mode, COM automation through Word or Excel, and even Notepad-driven fetches that shift network activity away from powershell.exe. Obfuscation goes beyond Invoke-Obfuscation’s token tricks: wildcarded cmdlet and method resolution, varied invocation paths such as runspaces and workflows, and aggressive IEX concatenation built by enumerating string members across PowerShell 2 through 5.

For defenders he stresses behavior over brittle string matching: parent-child process anomalies, svchost and Office-initiated connections, compilation via csc.exe, AMSI limits, registry artifacts from WinHTTP loads, and cache remnants. A live demo walks the tool’s color-coded menus, artifact hints per cradle, and randomized obfuscation options. He closes by urging log upgrades, incremental detection wins, and sharing failures so red and blue teams keep pace with evolving cradle shapes.

talks.title: 12. Enhancing Your Threat Simulation by 4n6ir
talks.teaser: Shows how accurate threat actor emulation by red teams can sharpen blue team detections and measurable defensive outcomes.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that red and blue teams do better as partners than rivals, and that threat simulation is only useful when it reproduces how real actors behave. The speaker compared two obfuscated PowerShell download cradles whose aliasing and ordering differed, showing they came from different advanced persistent threat groups, so a red teamer must know which actor they are imitating. Defenders gain more from behavioral signals than from obfuscation. Clustering named pipes by length and entropy quickly exposed a default Cobalt Strike Beacon pipe.

On the detection side, the speaker described a Windows share-access gap: scanners that only check whether a share exists leave the relative target name empty, which exposed PowerView and BloodHound style enumeration. For reporting, the speaker favored value metrics such as time to compromise and time to detect over counts of shells or domain admin hits. Findings should be mapped onto the kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK with simple grading, and BITS was presented as a built-in transfer and exfiltration method, caught by flagging first-seen domains.

The closing advice was that bottom-of-the-pyramid indicators like IPs and domains lose value in cloud environments, so teams should focus on TTPs and target-centric analysis. Red teams should get the same tool access as defenders, push tactical findings directly into engineering backlogs, and join blue teams on shared projects. The speaker noted that a three-minute path from hands-on-keyboard to exfiltration was the fastest seen, measured against the two-hour detection targets many teams set.

talks.title: 11. Where Cypherpunk Meets Organized Crime by Ben Brown
talks.teaser: Traces financially motivated electronic crime from early wire fraud and phone phreaking to modern dark net markets.
talks.summary:
The talk traces financially motivated electronic crime from its earliest roots to today's dark web. It opens with 19th-century telegraph wire fraud, then covers 1960s purchasing fraud over electronic data interchange, 1970s phone phreaking with blue boxes, and a 1972 drug deal arranged over ARPANET as an early precursor to online marketplaces.

The middle section follows bulletin boards, Usenet spam and bot wars, IRC culture and hacker groups through the 1980s and 1990s, plus government responses such as Operation Sun Devil. It explains how 1990s cryptography export limits shaped online commerce, then moves through carding forums, gold-backed and later cryptocurrencies, and privacy networks such as Tor, I2P and Freenet. Early dark net markets, from Farmers Market to Silk Road, close this part, and the speaker points out that Bitcoin's public ledger undermines claims of full anonymity.

The closing section covers an FBI operation against a child abuse forum that used one warrant to hack users in many countries, and the policy fights that followed over hacking warrant rules and the UK Investigatory Powers Act. The speaker frames these as a possible second crypto war. The main takeaway is that criminal methods tend to repeat as technology changes, so practitioners should watch how encryption and hacking laws evolve.
